title: The fingers will testify
hook: the Prophet ﷺ counted praises on his fingers, saying they'd be asked and made to speak (Tirmidhi)

segments.voice: Yesterday: one whole prayer, fajr, takbir to taslim. Your line was the whole thing. Did you catch the gray sky at dawn? Day one hundred thirteen.

Look at your hands for a second. Think about what they did yesterday. Typed. Scrolled. Held a cup. Maybe held someone's hand. Maybe made a fist. Maybe tapped a car horn a little harder than they needed to. Your hands keep a record you don't think about. Now picture a man sitting after the prayer is done, his right hand resting on his knee, his thumb moving slowly from one finger joint to the next, his lips moving without sound. He isn't fidgeting. He's counting. And the reason for counting that way, on the fingers, is a little startling. Today: the fingers will testify.
screen: `YOUR HANDS KEEP A RECORD.` → `A THUMB MOVING JOINT TO JOINT.` → `HE'S COUNTING.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the prayer. This week opens what comes after it: dhikr, remembrance, the short phrases repeated after the prayer and through the day. And it starts with how they're counted. A hadith in the collection of at-Tirmidhi comes from a woman named Yusayrah, one of the early emigrants. She said the Prophet ﷺ told the women: hold on to glorifying God, and declaring His oneness and holiness, and count on your fingertips, for they will be asked, and made to speak. And don't be heedless, or you'll forget mercy. Asked and made to speak. That comes from the Qur'an. In Surah Ya Sin, it describes the Day of Judgment: mouths are sealed, and hands speak, and feet bear witness to what they earned. It's usually heard as a warning. The body will tell what it did. But this hadith turns it around. If the fingers will testify anyway, give them something good to say. Let them have counted glory. Another companion, Abdullah ibn Amr, said he saw the Prophet count his praises on his right hand. So many Muslims still do: thumb touching each joint in turn, three on each finger, fifteen on one hand. Prayer beads, a string of thirty-three or ninety-nine, came into wide use later, and most scholars count them as fine too. But the fingers were first. They're always with you. You can't leave them at home. And in the tradition, every count they keep becomes a witness in your favor.
screen: `THIS WEEK: DHIKR, REMEMBRANCE.` · `COUNT ON YOUR FINGERTIPS.` · `ASKED, AND MADE TO SPEAK.` · `GIVE THEM SOMETHING GOOD TO SAY.` · then, large: `THE FINGERS WERE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count ten on your right hand. Rest the hand, palm up. With your thumb, touch the lowest joint of your little finger. One. The middle joint. Two. The tip. Three. Then the ring finger, three more. Then the middle finger. Keep going until you reach ten. If you pray, you can say a short phrase of remembrance on each count, like subhanallah. If not, just say the numbers, slowly, and feel each joint. Then let the hand rest open. The bell holds the time.
The fingers will testify. Count your praises on your fingertips, the Prophet said, for they'll be asked and made to speak. Today's word.
Your line: the fingers remember. Once today, when your hand reaches for your phone for no reason, touch three finger joints instead, and count. Day one hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: After the prayer and through the day, many Muslims count short phrases of remembrance on the joints of the fingers of the right hand, following the Prophet's example; others use prayer beads.

fork.setup: you want to keep count of your remembrance after the prayer. what did the Prophet ﷺ tell the women to use?
fork.reveal: count on your fingertips, for they will be asked and made to speak (Tirmidhi, from Yusayrah).

original.note: Arabic: fingertips, the word in the hadith: count on the fingertips.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims count on their fingers to keep track.
what it means: in the hadith, the fingers will testify, so counting praise on them gives them good to say.
what a scholar hears: Yusayrah's hadith (Tirmidhi 3583) echoing Ya Sin 36:65; Abdullah ibn Amr's report of the right hand (Abu Dawud 1502).

sources.ref: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3583 (Yusayrah: count on your fingertips, for they will be asked and made to speak)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1502 (Abdullah ibn Amr: counting tasbih on the right hand)
Qur'an 36:65 (mouths sealed, hands speak, feet bear witness)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm. Yusayrah's hadith is graded hasan or similar by some, weaker by others.
'On his right hand' appears in some narrations of Abu Dawud 1502; please confirm the wording.
Prayer beads (subha, misbaha): most scholars permit; some prefer fingers. Stated as 'most scholars count them as fine'.
The finger-joint method (three per finger) is widespread practice, not stated in the hadith; presented as what many Muslims do.
